When a Flask application handles a request, it pushes a request context
to set the active application and request data. When it handles a CLI command,
it pushes an app context to set the active application. When the activity ends,
it pops that context. Proxy objects like :data:`.request`, :data:`.session`,
:data:`.g`, and :data:`.current_app`, are accessible while the context is pushed
and active, and are not accessible after the context is popped.
The context is unique to each thread (or other worker type). The proxies cannot
be passed to another worker, which has a different context space and will not
know about the active context in the parent's space.

Flask dispatches a request in multiple stages which can affect the request,
response, and how errors are handled. See :doc:`/lifecycle` for a list of all
the steps, callbacks, and signals during each request. The following are the
steps directly related to the context.
-   The app context is pushed, the proxies are available.
-   The app context is popped, the proxies are no longer available.
The teardown callbacks are called by the context when it is popped. They are
called even if there is an unhandled exception during dispatch. They may be
called multiple times in some test scenarios. This means there is no guarantee
that any other parts of the request dispatch have run. Be sure to write these
functions in a way that does not depend on other callbacks. All callbacks are
called even if any raise an error.

Async functions require an event loop to run. Flask, as a WSGI
application, uses one worker to handle one request/response cycle.
When a request comes in to an async view, Flask will start an event loop
in a thread, run the view function there, then return the result.
Each request still ties up one worker, even for async views. The upside
is that you can run async code within a view, for example to make
multiple concurrent database queries, HTTP requests to an external API,
etc. However, the number of requests your application can handle at one
**Async is not inherently faster than sync code.** Async is beneficial
when performing concurrent IO-bound tasks, but will probably not improve
CPU-bound tasks. Traditional Flask views will still be appropriate for
most use cases, but Flask's async support enables writing and using
code that wasn't possible natively before.
Async functions will run in an event loop until they complete, at
which stage the event loop will stop. This means any additional
spawned tasks that haven't completed when the async function completes
will be cancelled. Therefore you cannot spawn background tasks, for
If you wish to use background tasks it is best to use a task queue to
trigger background work, rather than spawn tasks in a view
function. With that in mind you can spawn asyncio tasks by serving
Flask with an ASGI server and utilising the asgiref WsgiToAsgi adapter
as described in :doc:`deploying/asgi`. This works as the adapter creates
an event loop that runs continually.
Flask's async support is less performant than async-first frameworks due
to the way it is implemented. If you have a mainly async codebase it
would make sense to consider `Quart`_. Quart is a reimplementation of
Flask based on the `ASGI`_ standard instead of WSGI. This allows it to
handle many concurrent requests, long running requests, and websockets
without requiring multiple worker processes or threads.
It has also already been possible to :doc:`run Flask with Gevent </gevent>` to
get many of the benefits of async request handling. Gevent patches low-level
Python functions to accomplish this, whereas ``async``/``await`` and ASGI use
standard, modern Python capabilities. Deciding whether you should use gevent
with Flask, or Quart, or something else is ultimately up to understanding the
Flask extensions predating Flask's async support do not expect async views.
If they provide decorators to add functionality to views, those will probably
not work with async views because they will not await the function or be
awaitable. Other functions they provide will not be awaitable either and
will probably be blocking if called within an async view.

Flask uses a concept of *blueprints* for making application components and
supporting common patterns within an application or across applications.
Blueprints can greatly simplify how large applications work and provide a
central means for Flask extensions to register operations on applications.
A :class:`Blueprint` object works similarly to a :class:`Flask`
application object, but it is not actually an application.  Rather it is a
*blueprint* of how to construct or extend an application.
Blueprints in Flask are intended for these cases:
* Factor an application into a set of blueprints.  This is ideal for
larger applications; a project could instantiate an application object,
initialize several extensions, and register a collection of blueprints.
* Register a blueprint on an application at a URL prefix and/or subdomain.
Parameters in the URL prefix/subdomain become common view arguments
(with defaults) across all view functions in the blueprint.
* Register a blueprint multiple times on an application with different URL
* Provide template filters, static files, templates, and other utilities
through blueprints.  A blueprint does not have to implement applications
* Register a blueprint on an application for any of these cases when

You can use the :meth:`flask.Flask.route` decorator. 535|2. You can use the :meth:`flask.Flask.add_url_rule` function. 536|3. You can directly access the underlying Werkzeug routing system 537| which is exposed as :attr:`flask.Flask.url_map`. 538| 539|Variable parts in the route can be specified with angular brackets 540|(``/user/``). By default a variable part in the URL accepts any 541|string without a slash however a different converter can be specified as 542|well by using ````. 543| 544|Variable parts are passed to the view function as keyword arguments. 545| 546|The following converters are available: 547| 548|=========== =============================================== 549|`string` accepts any text without a slash (the default) 550|`int` accepts integers 551|`float` like `int` but for floating point values 552|`path` like the default but also accepts slashes 553|`any` matches one of the items provided 554|`uuid` accepts UUID strings 555|=========== =============================================== 556| 557|Custom converters can be defined using :attr:`flask.Flask.url_map`. 558| 559|Here are some examples:: 560| 561| @app.route('/') 562| def index(): 563| pass 564| 565| @app.route('/') 566| def show_user(username): 567| pass 568| 569| @app.route('/post/') 570| def show_post(post_id): 571| pass 572| 573|An important detail to keep in mind is how Flask deals with trailing 574|slashes. The idea is to keep each URL unique so the following rules 575|apply: 576| 577|1. If a rule ends with a slash and is requested without a slash by the 578| user, the user is automatically redirected to the same page with a 579| trailing slash attached. 580|2. If a rule does not end with a trailing slash and the user requests the 581| page with a trailing slash, a 404 not found is raised. 582| 583|This is consistent with how web servers deal with static files. This 584|also makes it possible to use relative link targets safely. 585| 586|You can also define multiple rules for the same function. They have to be 587|unique however. Defaults can also be specified. Here for example is a 588|definition for a URL that accepts an optional page:: 589| 590| @app.route('/users/', defaults={'page': 1}) 591| @app.route('/users/page/') 592| def show_users(page): 593| pass 594| 595|This specifies that ``/users/`` will be the URL for page one and 596|``/users/page/N`` will be the URL for page ``N``. 597| 598|If a URL contains a default value, it will be redirected to its simpler 599|form with a 308 redirect. In the above example, ``/users/page/1`` will 600|be redirected to ``/users/``. If your route handles ``GET`` and ``POST`` 601|requests, make sure the default route only handles ``GET``, as redirects 602|can't preserve form data. :: 603| 604| @app.route('/region/', defaults={'id': 1}) 605| @app.route('/region/', methods=['GET', 'POST']) 606| def region(id): 607| pass 608| 609|Here are the parameters that :meth:`~flask.Flask.route` and 610|:meth:`~flask.Flask.add_url_rule` accept. The only difference is that 611|with the route parameter the view function is defined with the decorator 612|instead of the `view_func` parameter. 613| 614|=============== ========================================================== 615|`rule` the URL rule as string 616|`endpoint` the endpoint for the registered URL rule. Flask itself 617| assumes that the name of the view function is the name 618| of the endpoint if not explicitly stated. 619|`view_func` the function to call when serving a request to the 620| provided endpoint. If this is not provided one can 621| specify the function later by storing it in the 622| :attr:`~flask.Flask.view_functions` dictionary with the 623| endpoint as key. 624|`defaults` A dictionary with defaults for this rule. See the 625| example above for how defaults work. 626|`subdomain` specifies the rule for the subdomain in case subdomain 627| matching is in use. If not specified the default 628| subdomain is assumed. 629|`**options` the options to be forwarded to the underlying 630| :class:`~werkzeug.routing.Rule` object. A change to 631| Werkzeug is handling of method options. methods is a list 632| of methods this rule should be limited to (``GET``, ``POST`` 633| etc.). By default a rule just listens for ``GET`` (and 634| implicitly ``HEAD``). Starting with Flask 0.6, ``OPTIONS`` is 635| implicitly added and handled by the standard request 636| handling. Rather than passing this data around to every function, the 6|:data:`.current_app`, :data:`.g`, :data:`.request`, and :data:`.session` proxies 7|are accessed instead. 8| 9|When handling a request, the context is referred to as the "request context" 10|because it contains request data in addition to application data. Otherwise, 11|such as during a CLI command, it is referred to as the "app context". During an 12|app context, :data:`.current_app` and :data:`.g` are available, while during a 13|request context :data:`.request` and :data:`.session` are also available. 14| 15| 16|Purpose of the Context 17|---------------------- 18| 19|The context and proxies help solve two development issues: circular imports, and 20|passing around global data during a request. 21| 22|The :class:`.Flask` application object has attributes, such as 23|:attr:`~.Flask.config`, that are useful to access within views and other 24|functions. However, importing the ``app`` instance within the modules in your 25|project is prone to circular import issues. When using the 26|:doc:`app factory pattern ` or writing reusable 27|:doc:`blueprints ` or :doc:`extensions ` there won't 28|be an ``app`` instance to import at all. 29| 30|When the application handles a request, it creates a :class:`.Request` object. 31|Because a *worker* handles only one request at a time, the request data can be 32|considered global to that worker during that request. Passing it as an argument 33|through every function during the request becomes verbose and redundant. 34| 35|Flask solves these issues with the *active context* pattern. Rather than 36|importing an ``app`` directly, or having to pass it and the request through to 37|every single function, you import and access the proxies, which point to the 38|currently active application and request data. This is sometimes referred to 39|as "context local" data. 40| 41| 42|Context During Setup 43|-------------------- 44| 45|If you try to access :data:`.current_app`, :data:`.g`, or anything that uses it, 46|outside an app context, you'll get this error message: 47| 48|.. code-block:: pytb 49| 50| RuntimeError: Working outside of application context. 51| 52| Attempted to use functionality that expected a current application to be 53| set. To solve this, set up an app context using 'with app.app_context()'. 54| See the documentation on app context for more information. 55| 56|If you see that error while configuring your application, such as when 57|initializing an extension, you can push a context manually since you have direct 58|access to the ``app``. Use :meth:`.Flask.app_context` in a ``with`` block. 59| 60|.. code-block:: python 61| 62| def create_app(): 63| app = Flask(__name__) 64| 65| with app.app_context(): 66| init_db() 67| 68| return app 69| 70|If you see that error somewhere else in your code not related to setting up the 71|application, it most likely indicates that you should move that code into a view 72|function or CLI command. 73| 74| 75|Context During Testing 76|---------------------- 77| 78|See :doc:`/testing` for detailed information about managing the context during 79|tests. 80| 81|If you try to access :data:`.request`, :data:`.session`, or anything that uses 82|it, outside a request context, you'll get this error message: 83| 84|.. code-block:: pytb 85| 86| RuntimeError: Working outside of request context. 87| 88| Attempted to use functionality that expected an active HTTP request. See the 89| documentation on request context for more information. 90| 91|This will probably only happen during tests. If you see that error somewhere 92|else in your code not related to testing, it most likely indicates that you 93|should move that code into a view function. 94| 95|The primary way to solve this is to use :meth:`.Flask.test_client` to simulate 96|a full request. 97| 98|If you only want to unit test one function, rather than a full request, use 99|:meth:`.Flask.test_request_context` in a ``with`` block. 100| 101|.. code-block:: python 102| 103| def generate_report(year): 104| format = request.args.get("format") 105| ... 106| 107| with app.test_request_context( 108| "/make_report/2017", query_string={"format": "short"} 109| ): 110| generate_report() 111| 112| 113|.. _context-visibility: 114| 115|Visibility of the Context 116|------------------------- 117| 118|The context will have the same lifetime as an activity, such as a request, CLI 119|command, or ``with`` block. Various callbacks and signals registered with the 120|app will be run during the context. 121| 122|When a Flask application handles a request, it pushes a request context 123|to set the active application and request data. When it handles a CLI command, 124|it pushes an app context to set the active application. When the activity ends, 125|it pops that context. Proxy objects like :data:`.request`, :data:`.session`, 126|:data:`.g`, and :data:`.current_app`, are accessible while the context is pushed 127|and active, and are not accessible after the context is popped. 128| 129|The context is unique to each thread (or other worker type). The proxies cannot 130|be passed to another worker, which has a different context space and will not 131|know about the active context in the parent's space. 132| 133|Besides being scoped to each worker, the proxy object has a separate type and 134|identity than the proxied real object. In some cases you'll need access to the 135|real object, rather than the proxy. Use the 136|:meth:`~.LocalProxy._get_current_object` method in those cases. 137| 138|.. code-block:: python 139| 140| app = current_app._get_current_object() 141| my_signal.send(app) 142| 143| 144|Lifecycle of the Context 145|------------------------ 146| 147|Flask dispatches a request in multiple stages which can affect the request, 148|response, and how errors are handled. See :doc:`/lifecycle` for a list of all 149|the steps, callbacks, and signals during each request. The following are the 150|steps directly related to the context. 151| 152|- The app context is pushed, the proxies are available. 153|- The :data:`.appcontext_pushed` signal is sent. 154|- The request is dispatched. 155|- Any :meth:`.Flask.teardown_request` decorated functions are called. 156|- The :data:`.request_tearing_down` signal is sent. 157|- Any :meth:`.Flask.teardown_appcontext` decorated functions are called. 158|- The :data:`.appcontext_tearing_down` signal is sent. 159|- The app context is popped, the proxies are no longer available. 160|- The :data:`.appcontext_popped` signal is sent. 161| 162|The teardown callbacks are called by the context when it is popped. They are 163|called even if there is an unhandled exception during dispatch. They may be 164|called multiple times in some test scenarios. This means there is no guarantee 165|that any other parts of the request dispatch have run. Be sure to write these 166|functions in a way that does not depend on other callbacks. All callbacks are 167|called even if any raise an error. 168| 169| 170|How the Context Works 171|--------------------- 172| 173|Context locals are implemented using Python's :mod:`contextvars` and Werkzeug's 174|:class:`~werkzeug.local.LocalProxy`. Python's contextvars are a low level 175|structure to manage data local to a thread or coroutine. ``LocalProxy`` wraps 176|the contextvar so that access to any attributes and methods is forwarded to the 177|object stored in the contextvar. 178| 179|The context is tracked like a stack, with the active context at the top of the 180|stack. Flask manages pushing and popping contexts during requests, CLI commands, 181|testing, ``with`` blocks, etc. The proxies access attributes on the active 182|context. 183| 184|Because it is a stack, other contexts may be pushed to change the proxies during 185|an already active context. This is not a common pattern, but can be used in 186|advanced use cases. For example, a Flask application can be used as WSGI 187|middleware, calling another wrapped Flask app from a view. --- END FILE: docs/appcontext.rst --- --- FILE: src/flask/ctx.py --- 1|from __future__ import annotations 2| 3|import contextvars 4|import typing as t 5|from functools import update_wrapper 6|from types import TracebackType 7| 8|from werkzeug.exceptions import HTTPException 9|from werkzeug.routing import MapAdapter 10| 11|from . import typing as ft 12|from .globals import _cv_app 13|from .helpers import _CollectErrors 14|from .signals import appcontext_popped 15|from .signals import appcontext_pushed 16| 17|if t.TYPE_CHECKING: 18| import typing_extensions as te 19| from _typeshed.wsgi import WSGIEnvironment 20| 21| from .app import Flask 22| from .sessions import SessionMixin 23| from .wrappers import Request 24| 25| 26|# a singleton sentinel value for parameter defaults 27|_sentinel = object() 28| 29| 30|class _AppCtxGlobals: 31| """A plain object. This allows views to be 11|defined with ``async def`` and use ``await``. 12| 13|.. code-block:: python 14| 15| @app.route("/get-data") 16| async def get_data(): 17| data = await async_db_query(...) 18| return jsonify(data) 19| 20|Pluggable class-based views also support handlers that are implemented as 21|coroutines. This applies to the :meth:`~flask.views.View.dispatch_request` 22|method in views that inherit from the :class:`flask.views.View` class, as 23|well as all the HTTP method handlers in views that inherit from the 24|:class:`flask.views.MethodView` class. 25| 26| 27|Performance 28|----------- 29| 30|Async functions require an event loop to run. Flask, as a WSGI 31|application, uses one worker to handle one request/response cycle. 32|When a request comes in to an async view, Flask will start an event loop 33|in a thread, run the view function there, then return the result. 34| 35|Each request still ties up one worker, even for async views. The upside 36|is that you can run async code within a view, for example to make 37|multiple concurrent database queries, HTTP requests to an external API, 38|etc. However, the number of requests your application can handle at one 39|time will remain the same. 40| 41|**Async is not inherently faster than sync code.** Async is beneficial 42|when performing concurrent IO-bound tasks, but will probably not improve 43|CPU-bound tasks. Traditional Flask views will still be appropriate for 44|most use cases, but Flask's async support enables writing and using 45|code that wasn't possible natively before. 46| 47| 48|Background tasks 49|---------------- 50| 51|Async functions will run in an event loop until they complete, at 52|which stage the event loop will stop. This means any additional 53|spawned tasks that haven't completed when the async function completes 54|will be cancelled. Therefore you cannot spawn background tasks, for 55|example via ``asyncio.create_task``. 56| 57|If you wish to use background tasks it is best to use a task queue to 58|trigger background work, rather than spawn tasks in a view 59|function. With that in mind you can spawn asyncio tasks by serving 60|Flask with an ASGI server and utilising the asgiref WsgiToAsgi adapter 61|as described in :doc:`deploying/asgi`. This works as the adapter creates 62|an event loop that runs continually. 63| 64| 65|When to use Quart instead 66|------------------------- 67| 68|Flask's async support is less performant than async-first frameworks due 69|to the way it is implemented. If you have a mainly async codebase it 70|would make sense to consider `Quart`_. Quart is a reimplementation of 71|Flask based on the `ASGI`_ standard instead of WSGI. This allows it to 72|handle many concurrent requests, long running requests, and websockets 73|without requiring multiple worker processes or threads. 74| 75|It has also already been possible to :doc:`run Flask with Gevent ` to 76|get many of the benefits of async request handling. Gevent patches low-level 77|Python functions to accomplish this, whereas ``async``/``await`` and ASGI use 78|standard, modern Python capabilities. Deciding whether you should use gevent 79|with Flask, or Quart, or something else is ultimately up to understanding the 80|specific needs of your project. 81| 82|.. _Quart: https://quart.palletsprojects.com 83|.. _ASGI: https://asgi.readthedocs.io 84| 85| 86|Extensions 87|---------- 88| 89|Flask extensions predating Flask's async support do not expect async views. 90|If they provide decorators to add functionality to views, those will probably 91|not work with async views because they will not await the function or be 92|awaitable. Other functions they provide will not be awaitable either and 93|will probably be blocking if called within an async view. 94| 95|Extension authors can support async functions by utilising the 96|:meth:`flask.Flask.ensure_sync` method. For example, if the extension 97|provides a view function decorator add ``ensure_sync`` before calling 98|the decorated function, 99| 100|.. code-block:: python 101| 102| def extension(func): 103| @wraps(func) 104| def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): 105| ... # Extension logic 106| return current_app.ensure_sync(func)(*args, **kwargs) 107| 108| return wrapper 109| 110|Check the changelog of the extension you want to use to see if they've 111|implemented async support, or make a feature request or PR to them. 112| 113| 114|Other event loops 115|----------------- 116| 117|At the moment Flask only supports :mod:`asyncio`. It's possible to override 118|:meth:`flask.Flask.ensure_sync` to change how async functions are wrapped to use 119|a different library. See :ref:`gevent-asyncio` for an example. --- END FILE: docs/async-await.rst --- --- FILE: src/flask/debughelpers.py --- 1|from __future__ import annotations 2| 3|import typing as t 4| 5|from jinja2.loaders import BaseLoader 6|from werkzeug.routing import RequestRedirect 7| 8|from .blueprints import Blueprint 9|from .globals import _cv_app 10|from .sansio.app import App 11| 12|if t.TYPE_CHECKING: 13| from .sansio.scaffold import Scaffold 14| from .wrappers import Request 15| 16| 17|class UnexpectedUnicodeError(AssertionError, UnicodeError): 18| """Raised in places where we want some better error reporting for 19| unexpected unicode or binary data. 20| """ 21| 22| 23|class DebugFilesKeyError(KeyError, AssertionError): 24| """Raised from request.files during debugging. 3| 4|.. currentmodule:: flask 5| 6|.. versionadded:: 0.7 7| 8|Flask uses a concept of *blueprints* for making application components and 9|supporting common patterns within an application or across applications. 10|Blueprints can greatly simplify how large applications work and provide a 11|central means for Flask extensions to register operations on applications. 12|A :class:`Blueprint` object works similarly to a :class:`Flask` 13|application object, but it is not actually an application. Rather it is a 14|*blueprint* of how to construct or extend an application. 15| 16|Why Blueprints? 17|--------------- 18| 19|Blueprints in Flask are intended for these cases: 20| 21|* Factor an application into a set of blueprints. This is ideal for 22| larger applications; a project could instantiate an application object, 23| initialize several extensions, and register a collection of blueprints. 24|* Register a blueprint on an application at a URL prefix and/or subdomain. 25| Parameters in the URL prefix/subdomain become common view arguments 26| (with defaults) across all view functions in the blueprint. 27|* Register a blueprint multiple times on an application with different URL 28| rules. 29|* Provide template filters, static files, templates, and other utilities 30| through blueprints. A blueprint does not have to implement applications 31| or view functions. 32|* Register a blueprint on an application for any of these cases when 33| initializing a Flask extension. 34| 35|A blueprint in Flask is not a pluggable app because it is not actually an 36|application -- it's a set of operations which can be registered on an 37|application, even multiple times. Why not have multiple application 38|objects? You can do that (see :doc:`/patterns/appdispatch`), but your 39|applications will have separate configs and will be managed at the WSGI 40|layer. 41| 42|Blueprints instead provide separation at the Flask level, share 43|application config, and can change an application object as necessary with 44|being registered. The downside is that you cannot unregister a blueprint 45|once an application was created without having to destroy the whole 46|application object. 47| 48|The Concept of Blueprints 49|------------------------- 50| 51|The basic concept of blueprints is that they record operations to execute 52|when registered on an application. Flask associates view functions with 53|blueprints when dispatching requests and generating URLs from one endpoint 54|to another. 55| 56|My First Blueprint 57|------------------ 58| 59|This is what a very basic blueprint looks like. In this case we want to 60|implement a blueprint that does simple rendering of static templates:: 61| 62| from flask import Blueprint, render_template, abort 63| from jinja2 import TemplateNotFound 64| 65| simple_page = Blueprint('simple_page', __name__, 66| template_folder='templates') 67| 68| @simple_page.route('/', defaults={'page': 'index'}) 69| @simple_page.route('/') 70| def show(page): 71| try: 72| return render_template(f'pages/{page}.html') 73| except TemplateNotFound: 74| abort(404) 75| 76|When you bind a function with the help of the ``@simple_page.route`` 77|decorator, the blueprint will record the intention of registering the 78|function ``show`` on the application when it's later registered. 79|Additionally it will prefix the endpoint of the function with the 80|name of the blueprint which was given to the :class:`Blueprint` 81|constructor (in this case also ``simple_page``). The blueprint's name 82|does not modify the URL, only the endpoint. 83| 84|Registering Blueprints 85|---------------------- 86| 87|So how do you register that blueprint? Like this:: 88| 89| from flask import Flask 90| from yourapplication.simple_page import simple_page 91| 92| app = Flask(__name__) 93| app.register_blueprint(simple_page) 94| 95|If you check the rules registered on the application, you will find 96|these:: 97| 98| >>> app.url_map 99| Map([' (HEAD, OPTIONS, GET) -> static>, 100| ' (HEAD, OPTIONS, GET) -> simple_page.show>, 101| simple_page.show>]) 102| 103|The first one is obviously from the application itself for the static 104|files. The other two are for the `show` function of the ``simple_page`` 105|blueprint. As you can see, they are also prefixed with the name of the 106|blueprint and separated by a dot (``.``). 107| 108|Blueprints however can also be mounted at different locations:: 109| 110| app.register_blueprint(simple_page, url_prefix='/pages') 111| 112|And sure enough, these are the generated rules:: 113| 114| >>> app.url_map 115| Map([' (HEAD, OPTIONS, GET) -> static>, 116| ' (HEAD, OPTIONS, GET) -> simple_page.show>, 117| simple_page.show>]) 118| 119|On top of that you can register blueprints multiple times though not every 120|blueprint might respond properly to that. In fact it depends on how the 121|blueprint is implemented if it can be mounted more than once. 122| 123|Nesting Blueprints 124|------------------ 125| 126|It is possible to register a blueprint on another blueprint. 127| 128|.. code-block:: python 129| 130| parent = Blueprint('parent', __name__, url_prefix='/parent') 131| child = Blueprint('child', __name__, url_prefix='/child') 132| parent.register_blueprint(child) 133| app.register_blueprint(parent) 134| 135|The child blueprint will gain the parent's name as a prefix to its 136|name, and child URLs will be prefixed with the parent's URL prefix. 137| 138|.. code-block:: python 139| 140| url_for('parent.child.create') 141| /parent/child/create 142| 143|In addition a child blueprint's will gain their parent's subdomain, 144|with their subdomain as prefix if present i.e. 145| 146|.. code-block:: python 147| 148| parent = Blueprint('parent', __name__, subdomain='parent') 149| child = Blueprint('child', __name__, subdomain='child') 150| parent.register_blueprint(child) 151| app.register_blueprint(parent) 152| 153| url_for('parent.child.create', _external=True) 154| "child.parent.domain.tld" 155| 156|Blueprint-specific before request functions, etc. registered with the 157|parent will trigger for the child. If a child does not have an error 158|handler that can handle a given exception, the parent's will be tried. 159| 160| 161|Blueprint Resources 162|------------------- 163| 164|Blueprints can provide resources as well. Sometimes you might want to 165|introduce a blueprint only for the resources it provides. 166| 167|Blueprint Resource Folder 168|````````````````````````` 169| 170|Like for regular applications, blueprints are considered to be contained 171|in a folder. While multiple blueprints can originate from the same folder, 172|it does not have to be the case and it's usually not recommended. 173| 174|The folder is inferred from the second argument to :class:`Blueprint` which 175|is usually `__name__`. This argument specifies what logical Python 176|module or package corresponds to the blueprint. If it points to an actual 177|Python package that package (which is a folder on the filesystem) is the 178|resource folder. If it's a module, the package the module is contained in 179|will be the resource folder. You can access the 180|:attr:`Blueprint.root_path` property to see what the resource folder is:: 181| 182| >>> simple_page.root_path 183| '/Users/username/TestProject/yourapplication' 184| 185|To quickly open sources from this folder you can use the 186|:meth:`~Blueprint.open_resource` function:: 187| 188| with simple_page.open_resource('static/style.css') as f: 189| code = f.read() 190| 191|Static Files 192|```````````` 193| 194|A blueprint can expose a folder with static files by providing the path 195|to the folder on the filesystem with the ``static_folder`` argument. 196|It is either an absolute path or relative to the blueprint's location:: 197| 198| admin = Blueprint('admin', __name__, static_folder='static') 199| 200|By default the rightmost part of the path is where it is exposed on the 201|web. This can be changed with the ``static_url_path`` argument. Because the 202|folder is called ``static`` here it will be available at the 203|``url_prefix`` of the blueprint + ``/static``. If the blueprint 204|has the prefix ``/admin``, the static URL will be ``/admin/static``. 205| 206|The endpoint is named ``blueprint_name.static``. You can generate URLs 207|to it with :func:`url_for` like you would with the static folder of the 208|application:: 209| 210| url_for('admin.static', filename='style.css') 211| 212|However, if the blueprint does not have a ``url_prefix``, it is not 213|possible to access the blueprint's static folder. This is because the 214|URL would be ``/static`` in this case, and the application's ``/static`` 215|route takes precedence. Unlike template folders, blueprint static 216|folders are not searched if the file does not exist in the application 217|static folder. 218| 219|Templates 220|````````` 221| 222|If you want the blueprint to expose templates you can do that by providing 223|the `template_folder` parameter to the :class:`Blueprint` constructor:: 224| 225| admin = Blueprint('admin', __name__, template_folder='templates') 226| 227|For static files, the path can be absolute or relative to the blueprint 228|resource folder. 229| 230|The template folder is added to the search path of templates but with a lower 231|priority than the actual application's template folder. That way you can 232|easily override templates that a blueprint provides in the actual application. 233|This also means that if you don't want a blueprint template to be accidentally 234|overridden, make sure that no other blueprint or actual application template 235|has the same relative path. When multiple blueprints provide the same relative 236|template path the first blueprint registered takes precedence over the others. 237| 238| 239|So if you have a blueprint in the folder ``yourapplication/admin`` and you 240|want to render the template ``'admin/index.html'`` and you have provided 241|``templates`` as a `template_folder` you will have to create a file like 242|this: :file:`yourapplication/admin/templates/admin/index.html`. The reason 243|for the extra ``admin`` folder is to avoid getting our template overridden 244|by a template named ``index.html`` in the actual application template 245|folder. 246| 247|To further reiterate this: if you have a blueprint named ``admin`` and you 248|want to render a template called :file:`index.html` which is specific to this 249|blueprint, the best idea is to lay out your templates like this:: 250| 251| yourpackage/ 252| blueprints/ 253| admin/ 254| templates/ 255| admin/ 256| index.html 257| __init__.py 258| 259|And then when you want to render the template, use :file:`admin/index.html` as 260|the name to look up the template by. If you encounter problems loading 261|the correct templates enable the ``EXPLAIN_TEMPLATE_LOADING`` config 262|variable which will instruct Flask to print out the steps it goes through 263|to locate templates on every ``render_template`` call. 264| 265|Building URLs 266|------------- 267| 268|If you want to link from one page to another you can use the 269|:func:`url_for` function just like you normally would do just that you 270|prefix the URL endpoint with the name of the blueprint and a dot (``.``):: 271| 272| url_for('admin.index') 273| 274|Additionally if you are in a view function of a blueprint or a rendered 275|template and you want to link to another endpoint of the same blueprint, 276|you can use relative redirects by prefixing the endpoint with a dot only:: 277| 278| url_for('.index') 279| 280|This will link to ``admin.index`` for instance in case the current request 281|was dispatched to any other admin blueprint endpoint. 282| 283| 284|Blueprint Error Handlers 285|------------------------ 286| 287|Blueprints support the ``errorhandler`` decorator just like the :class:`Flask` 288|application object, so it is easy to make Blueprint-specific custom error 289|pages. 290| 291|Here is an example for a "404 Page Not Found" exception:: 292| 293| @simple_page.errorhandler(404) 294| def page_not_found(e): 295| return render_template('pages/404.html') 296| 297|Most error handlers will simply work as expected; however, there is a caveat 298|concerning handlers for 404 and 405 exceptions. These error handlers are only 299|invoked from an appropriate ``raise`` statement or a call to ``abort`` in another 300|of the blueprint's view functions; they are not invoked by, e.g., an invalid URL 301|access. This is because the blueprint does not "own" a certain URL space, so 302|the application instance has no way of knowing which blueprint error handler it 303|should run if given an invalid URL. Executed from the terminal, this script gives 8|access to built-in, extension, and application-defined commands. The ``--help`` 9|option will give more information about any commands and options. 10| 11|.. _Click: https://click.palletsprojects.com/ 12| 13| 14|Application Discovery 15|--------------------- 16| 17|The ``flask`` command is installed by Flask, not your application; it must be 18|told where to find your application in order to use it. The ``--app`` 19|option is used to specify how to load the application. 20| 21|While ``--app`` supports a variety of options for specifying your 22|application, most use cases should be simple. Here are the typical values: 23| 24|(nothing) 25| The name "app" or "wsgi" is imported (as a ".py" file, or package), 26| automatically detecting an app (``app`` or ``application``) or 27| factory (``create_app`` or ``make_app``). 28| 29|``--app hello`` 30| The given name is imported, automatically detecting an app (``app`` 31| or ``application``) or factory (``create_app`` or ``make_app``). 32| 33|---- 34| 35|``--app`` has three parts: an optional path that sets the current working 36|directory, a Python file or dotted import path, and an optional variable 37|name of the instance or factory. If the name is a factory, it can optionally 38|be followed by arguments in parentheses. The following values demonstrate these 39|parts: 40| 41|``--app src/hello`` 42| Sets the current working directory to ``src`` then imports ``hello``. 43| 44|``--app hello.web`` 45| Imports the path ``hello.web``. 46| 47|``--app hello:app2`` 48| Uses the ``app2`` Flask instance in ``hello``. 49| 50|``--app 'hello:create_app("dev")'`` 51| The ``create_app`` factory in ``hello`` is called with the string ``'dev'`` 52| as the argument. 53| 54|If ``--app`` is not set, the command will try to import "app" or 55|"wsgi" (as a ".py" file, or package) and try to detect an application 56|instance or factory. 57| 58|Within the given import, the command looks for an application instance named 59|``app`` or ``application``, then any application instance. If no instance is 60|found, the command looks for a factory function named ``create_app`` or 61|``make_app`` that returns an instance. 62| 63|If parentheses follow the factory name, their contents are parsed as 64|Python literals and passed as arguments and keyword arguments to the 65|function. This means that strings must still be in quotes. 66| 67| 68|Run the Development Server 69|-------------------------- 70| 71|The :func:`run ` command will start the development server. It 72|replaces the :meth:`Flask.run` method in most cases. :: 73| 74| $ flask --app hello run 75| * Serving Flask app "hello" 76| * Running on http://127.0.0.1:5000/ (Press CTRL+C to quit) 77| 78|.. warning:: Do not use this command to run your application in production. 79| Only use the development server during development. The development server 80| is provided for convenience, but is not designed to be particularly secure, 81| stable, or efficient. See :doc:`/deploying/index` for how to run in production. 82| 83|If another program is already using port 5000, you'll see 84|``OSError: [Errno 98]`` or ``OSError: [WinError 10013]`` when the 85|server tries to start. See :ref:`address-already-in-use` for how to 86|handle that. 87| 88| 89|Debug Mode 90|~~~~~~~~~~ 91| 92|In debug mode, the ``flask run`` command will enable the interactive debugger and the 93|reloader by default, and make errors easier to see and debug. To enable debug mode, use 94|the ``--debug`` option. 95| 96|.. code-block:: console 97| 98| $ flask --app hello run --debug 99| * Serving Flask app "hello" 100| * Debug mode: on 101| * Running on http://127.0.0.1:5000/ (Press CTRL+C to quit) 102| * Restarting with inotify reloader 103| * Debugger is active! 104| * Debugger PIN: 223-456-919 105| 106|The ``--debug`` option can also be passed to the top level ``flask`` command to enable 107|debug mode for any command. The following two ``run`` calls are equivalent. 108| 109|.. code-block:: console 110| 111| $ flask --app hello --debug run 112| $ flask --app hello run --debug 113| 114| 115|Watch and Ignore Files with the Reloader 116|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 117| 118|When using debug mode, the reloader will trigger whenever your Python code or imported 119|modules change. The reloader can watch additional files with the ``--extra-files`` 120|option. Multiple paths are separated with ``:``, or ``;`` on Windows. 121| 122|.. code-block:: text 123| 124| $ flask run --extra-files file1:dirA/file2:dirB/ 125| * Running on http://127.0.0.1:8000/ 126| * Detected change in '/path/to/file1', reloading 127| 128|The reloader can also ignore files using :mod:`fnmatch` patterns with the 129|``--exclude-patterns`` option. Multiple patterns are separated with ``:``, or ``;`` on 130|Windows. 131| 132| 133|Open a Shell 134|------------ 135| 136|To explore the data in your application, you can start an interactive Python 137|shell with the :func:`shell ` command. An application 138|context will be active, and the app instance will be imported. :: 139| 140| $ flask shell 141| Python 3.10.0 (default, Oct 27 2021, 06:59:51) [GCC 11.1.0] on linux 142| App: example [production] 143| Instance: /home/david/Projects/pallets/flask/instance 144| >>> 145| 146|Use :meth:`~Flask.shell_context_processor` to add other automatic imports. 147| 148| 149|.. _dotenv: 150| 151|Environment Variables From dotenv 152|--------------------------------- 153| 154|The ``flask`` command supports setting any option for any command with 155|environment variables. The variables are named like ``FLASK_OPTION`` or 156|``FLASK_COMMAND_OPTION``, for example ``FLASK_APP`` or 157|``FLASK_RUN_PORT``. 158| 159|Rather than passing options every time you run a command, or environment 160|variables every time you open a new terminal, you can use Flask's dotenv 161|support to set environment variables automatically. 162| 163|If `python-dotenv`_ is installed, running the ``flask`` command will set 164|environment variables defined in the files ``.env`` and ``.flaskenv``. 165|You can also specify an extra file to load with the ``--env-file`` 166|option. Dotenv files can be used to avoid having to set ``--app`` or 167|``FLASK_APP`` manually, and to set configuration using environment 168|variables similar to how some deployment services work. 169| 170|Variables set on the command line are used over those set in :file:`.env`, 171|which are used over those set in :file:`.flaskenv`. :file:`.flaskenv` should be 172|used for public variables, such as ``FLASK_APP``, while :file:`.env` should not 173|be committed to your repository so that it can set private variables. 174| 175|Directories are scanned upwards from the directory you call ``flask`` 176|from to locate the files. 177| 178|The files are only loaded by the ``flask`` command or calling 179|:meth:`~Flask.run`. If you would like to load these files when running in 180|production, you should call :func:`~cli.load_dotenv` manually. 181| 182|.. _python-dotenv: https://github.com/theskumar/python-dotenv#readme 183| 184| 185|Setting Command Options 186|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 187| 188|Click is configured to load default values for command options from 189|environment variables. The variables use the pattern 190|``FLASK_COMMAND_OPTION``. For example, to set the port for the run 191|command, instead of ``flask run --port 8000``: 192| 193|.. tabs:: 194| 195| .. group-tab:: Bash 196| 197| .. code-block:: text 198| 199| $ export FLASK_RUN_PORT=8000 200| $ flask run 201| * Running on http://127.0.0.1:8000/ 202| 203| .. group-tab:: Fish 204| 205| .. code-block:: text 206| 207| $ set -x FLASK_RUN_PORT 8000 208| $ flask run 209| * Running on http://127.0.0.1:8000/ 210| 211| .. group-tab:: CMD 212| 213| .. code-block:: text 214| 215| > set FLASK_RUN_PORT=8000 216| > flask run 217| * Running on http://127.0.0.1:8000/ 218| 219| .. group-tab:: Powershell 220| 221| .. code-block:: text 222| 223| > $env:FLASK_RUN_PORT = 8000 224| > flask run 225| * Running on http://127.0.0.1:8000/ 226| 227|These can be added to the ``.flaskenv`` file just like ``FLASK_APP`` to 228|control default command options. 229| 230| 231|Disable dotenv 232|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 233| 234|The ``flask`` command will show a message if it detects dotenv files but 235|python-dotenv is not installed. 236| 237|.. code-block:: bash 238| 239| $ flask run 240| * Tip: There are .env files present. Do "pip install python-dotenv" to use them. 241| 242|You can tell Flask not to load dotenv files even when python-dotenv is 243|installed by setting the ``FLASK_SKIP_DOTENV`` environment variable. 244|This can be useful if you want to load them manually, or if you're using 245|a project runner that loads them already. Keep in mind that the 246|environment variables must be set before the app loads or it won't 247|configure as expected. 248| 249|.. tabs:: 250| 251| .. group-tab:: Bash 252| 253| .. code-block:: text 254| 255| $ export FLASK_SKIP_DOTENV=1 256| $ flask run 257| 258| .. group-tab:: Fish 259| 260| .. code-block:: text 261| 262| $ set -x FLASK_SKIP_DOTENV 1 263| $ flask run 264| 265| .. group-tab:: CMD 266| 267| .. code-block:: text 268| 269| > set FLASK_SKIP_DOTENV=1 270| > flask run 271| 272| .. group-tab:: Powershell 273| 274| .. code-block:: text 275| 276| > $env:FLASK_SKIP_DOTENV = 1 277| > flask run 278| 279| 280|Environment Variables From virtualenv 281|------------------------------------- 282| 283|If you do not want to install dotenv support, you can still set environment 284|variables by adding them to the end of the virtualenv's :file:`activate` 285|script. Activating the virtualenv will set the variables. 286| 287|.. tabs:: 288| 289| .. group-tab:: Bash 290| 291| Unix Bash, :file:`.venv/bin/activate`:: 292| 293| $ export FLASK_APP=hello 294| 295| .. group-tab:: Fish 296| 297| Fish, :file:`.venv/bin/activate.fish`:: 298| 299| $ set -x FLASK_APP hello 300| 301| .. group-tab:: CMD 302| 303| Windows CMD, :file:`.venv\\Scripts\\activate.bat`:: 304| 305| > set FLASK_APP=hello 306| 307| .. group-tab:: Powershell 308| 309| Windows Powershell, :file:`.venv\\Scripts\\activate.ps1`:: 310| 311| > $env:FLASK_APP = "hello" 312| 313|It is preferred to use dotenv support over this, since :file:`.flaskenv` can be 314|committed to the repository so that it works automatically wherever the project 315|is checked out. 316| 317| 318|Custom Commands 319|--------------- 320| 321|The ``flask`` command is implemented using `Click`_. See that project's 322|documentation for full information about writing commands. 323| 324|This example adds the command ``create-user`` that takes the argument 325|``name``. :: 326| 327| import click 328| from flask import Flask 329| 330| app = Flask(__name__) 331| 332| @app.cli.command("create-user") 333| @click.argument("name") 334| def create_user(name): 335| ... 336| 337|:: 338| 339| $ flask create-user admin 340| 341|This example adds the same command, but as ``user create``, a command in a 342|group. This is useful if you want to organize multiple related commands. :: 343| 344| import click 345| from flask import Flask 346| from flask.cli import AppGroup 347| 348| app = Flask(__name__) 349| user_cli = AppGroup('user') 350| 351| @user_cli.command('create') 352| @click.argument('name') 353| def create_user(name): 354| ... 355| 356| app.cli.add_command(user_cli) 357| 358|:: 359| 360| $ flask user create demo 361| 362|See :ref:`testing-cli` for an overview of how to test your custom 363|commands. 364| 365| 366|Registering Commands with Blueprints 367|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 368| 369|If your application uses blueprints, you can optionally register CLI 370|commands directly onto them. When your blueprint is registered onto your 371|application, the associated commands will be available to the ``flask`` 372|command. By default, those commands will be nested in a group matching 373|the name of the blueprint. 374| 375|.. code-block:: python 376| 377| from flask import Blueprint 378| 379| bp = Blueprint('students', __name__) 380| 381| @bp.cli.command('create') 382| @click.argument('name') 383| def create(name): 384| ... 385| 386| app.register_blueprint(bp) 387| 388|.. code-block:: text 389| 390| $ flask students create alice 391| 392|You can alter the group name by specifying the ``cli_group`` parameter 393|when creating the :class:`Blueprint` object, or later with 394|:meth:`app.register_blueprint(bp, cli_group='...') `. 395|The following are equivalent: 396| 397|.. code-block:: python 398| 399| bp = Blueprint('students', __name__, cli_group='other') 400| # or 401| app.register_blueprint(bp, cli_group='other') 402| 403|.. code-block:: text 404| 405| $ flask other create alice 406| 407|Specifying ``cli_group=None`` will remove the nesting and merge the 408|commands directly to the application's level: 409| 410|.. code-block:: python 411| 412| bp = Blueprint('students', __name__, cli_group=None) 413| # or 414| app.register_blueprint(bp, cli_group=None) 415| 416|.. code-block:: text 417| 418| $ flask create alice 419| 420| 421|Application Context 422|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 423| 424|Commands added using the Flask app's :attr:`~Flask.cli` or 425|:class:`~flask.cli.FlaskGroup` :meth:`~cli.AppGroup.command` decorator 426|will be executed with an application context pushed, so your custom 427|commands and parameters have access to the app and its configuration. The 428|:func:`~cli.with_appcontext` decorator can be used to get the same 429|behavior, but is not needed in most cases. 430| 431|.. code-block:: python 432| 433| import click 434| from flask.cli import with_appcontext 435| 436| @click.command() 437| @with_appcontext 438| def do_work(): 439| ... 440| 441| app.cli.add_command(do_work) 442| 443| 444|Plugins 445|------- 446| 447|Flask will automatically load commands specified in the ``flask.commands`` 448|`entry point`_. This is useful for extensions that want to add commands when 449|they are installed. Entry points are specified in :file:`pyproject.toml`: 450| 451|.. code-block:: toml 452| 453| [project.entry-points."flask.commands"] 454| my-command = "my_extension.commands:cli" 455| 456|.. _entry point: https://packaging.python.org/tutorials/packaging-projects/#entry-points 457| 458|Inside :file:`my_extension/commands.py` you can then export a Click 459|object:: 460| 461| import click 462| 463| @click.command() 464| def cli(): 465| ... 466| 467|Once that package is installed in the same virtualenv as your Flask project, 468|you can run ``flask my-command`` to invoke the command. 469| 470| 471|.. _custom-scripts: 472| 473|Custom Scripts 474|-------------- 475| 476|When you are using the app factory pattern, it may be more convenient to define 477|your own Click script. Instead of using ``--app`` and letting Flask load 478|your application, you can create your own Click object and export it as a 479|`console script`_ entry point. 480| 481|Create an instance of :class:`~cli.FlaskGroup` and pass it the factory:: 482| 483| import click 484| from flask import Flask 485| from flask.cli import FlaskGroup 486| 487| def create_app(): 488| app = Flask('wiki') 489| # other setup 490| return app 491| 492| @click.group(cls=FlaskGroup, create_app=create_app) 493| def cli(): 494| """Management script for the Wiki application.""" 495| 496|Define the entry point in :file:`pyproject.toml`: 497| 498|.. code-block:: toml 499| 500| [project.scripts] 501| wiki = "wiki:cli" 502| 503|Install the application in the virtualenv in editable mode and the custom 504|script is available. Note that you don't need to set ``--app``. :: 505| 506| $ pip install -e . 507| $ wiki run 508| 509|.. admonition:: Errors in Custom Scripts 510| 511| When using a custom script, if you introduce an error in your 512| module-level code, the reloader will fail because it can no longer 513| load the entry point. 514| 515| The ``flask`` command, being separate from your code, does not have 516| this issue and is recommended in most cases. 517| 518|.. _console script: https://packaging.python.org/tutorials/packaging-projects/#console-scripts 519| 520| 521|PyCharm Integration 522|------------------- 523| 524|PyCharm Professional provides a special Flask run configuration to run the development 525|server. For the Community Edition, and for other commands besides ``run``, you need to 526|create a custom run configuration. These instructions should be similar for any other 527|IDE you use. 528| 529|In PyCharm, with your project open, click on *Run* from the menu bar and go to *Edit 530|Configurations*. You'll see a screen similar to this: 531| 532|.. image:: _static/pycharm-run-config.png 533| :align: center 534| :class: screenshot 535| :alt: Screenshot of PyCharm run configuration. 536| 537|Once you create a configuration for the ``flask run``, you can copy and change it to 538|call any other command. 539| 540|Click the *+ (Add New Configuration)* button and select *Python*. Give the configuration 541|a name such as "flask run". 542| 543|Click the *Script path* dropdown and change it to *Module name*, then input ``flask``. 544| 545|The *Parameters* field is set to the CLI command to execute along with any arguments. 546|This example uses ``--app hello run --debug``, which will run the development server in 547|debug mode. ``--app hello`` should be the import or file with your Flask app. 548| 549|If you installed your project as a package in your virtualenv, you may uncheck the 550|*PYTHONPATH* options. But 19|this is also where you can have your own configuration. 20| 21| 22|Configuration Basics 23|-------------------- 24| 25|The :attr:`~flask.Flask.config` is actually a subclass of a dictionary and 26|can be modified just like any dictionary:: 27| 28| app = Flask(__name__) 29| app.config['TESTING'] = True 30| 31|Certain configuration values are also forwarded to the 32|:attr:`~flask.Flask` object so you can read and write them from there:: 33| 34| app.testing = True 35| 36|To update multiple keys at once you can use the :meth:`dict.update` 37|method:: 38| 39| app.config.update( 40| TESTING=True, 41| SECRET_KEY='192b9bdd22ab9ed4d12e236c78afcb9a393ec15f71bbf5dc987d54727823bcbf' 42| ) 43| 44| 45|Debug Mode 46|---------- 47| 48|The :data:`DEBUG` config value is special because it may behave inconsistently if 49|changed after the app has begun setting up. In order to set debug mode reliably, use the 50|``--debug`` option on the ``flask`` or ``flask run`` command. ``flask run`` will use the 51|interactive debugger and reloader by default in debug mode. 52| 53|.. code-block:: text 54| 55| $ flask --app hello run --debug 56| 57|Using the option is recommended. While it is possible to set :data:`DEBUG` in your 58|config or code, this is strongly discouraged. It can't be read early by the 59|``flask run`` command, and some systems or extensions may have already configured 60|themselves based on a previous value. 61| 62| 63|Builtin Configuration Values 64|---------------------------- 65| 66|The following configuration values are used internally by Flask: 67| 68|.. py:data:: DEBUG 69| 70| Whether debug mode is enabled. When using ``flask run`` to start the development 71| server, an interactive debugger will be shown for unhandled exceptions, and the 72| server will be reloaded when code changes. The :attr:`~flask.Flask.debug` attribute 73| maps to this config key. This is set with the ``FLASK_DEBUG`` environment variable. 74| It may not behave as expected if set in code. 75| 76| **Do not enable debug mode when deploying in production.** 77| 78| Default: ``False`` 79| 80|.. py:data:: TESTING 81| 82| Enable testing mode. You can deploy your application, then 458|separately configure it for the specific deployment. 459| 460|A common pattern is this:: 461| 462| app = Flask(__name__) 463| app.config.from_object('yourapplication.default_settings') 464| app.config.from_envvar('YOURAPPLICATION_SETTINGS') 465| 466|This first loads the configuration from the 467|`yourapplication.default_settings` module and then overrides the values 468|with the contents of the file the :envvar:`YOURAPPLICATION_SETTINGS` 469|environment variable points to. This environment variable can be set 470|in the shell before starting the server: 471| 472|.. tabs:: 473| 474| .. group-tab:: Bash 475| 476| .. code-block:: text 477| 478| $ export YOURAPPLICATION_SETTINGS=/path/to/settings.cfg 479| $ flask run 480| * Running on http://127.0.0.1:5000/ 481| 482| .. group-tab:: Fish 483| 484| .. code-block:: text 485| 486| $ set -x YOURAPPLICATION_SETTINGS /path/to/settings.cfg 487| $ flask run 488| * Running on http://127.0.0.1:5000/ 489| 490| .. group-tab:: CMD 491| 492| .. code-block:: text 493| 494| > set YOURAPPLICATION_SETTINGS=\path\to\settings.cfg 495| > flask run 496| * Running on http://127.0.0.1:5000/ 497| 498| .. group-tab:: Powershell 499| 500| .. code-block:: text 501| 502| > $env:YOURAPPLICATION_SETTINGS = "\path\to\settings.cfg" 503| > flask run 504| * Running on http://127.0.0.1:5000/ 505| 506|The configuration files themselves are actual Python files. Only values 507|in uppercase are actually stored in the config object later on. So make 508|sure to use uppercase letters for your config keys. 509| 510|Here is an example of a configuration file:: 511| 512| # Example configuration 513| SECRET_KEY = '192b9bdd22ab9ed4d12e236c78afcb9a393ec15f71bbf5dc987d54727823bcbf' 514| 515|Make sure to load the configuration very early on, so that extensions have 516|the ability to access the configuration when starting up. There are other 517|methods on the config object as well to load from individual files. For a 518|complete reference, read the :class:`~flask.Config` object's 519|documentation. 520| 521| 522|Configuring from Data Files 523|--------------------------- 524| 525|It is also possible to load configuration from a file in a format of 526|your choice using :meth:`~flask.Config.from_file`. For example to load 527|from a TOML file: 528| 529|.. code-block:: python 530| 531| import tomllib 532| app.config.from_file("config.toml", load=tomllib.load, text=False) 533| 534|Or from a JSON file: 535| 536|.. code-block:: python 537| 538| import json 539| app.config.from_file("config.json", load=json.load) 540| 541| 542|Configuring from Environment Variables 543|-------------------------------------- 544| 545|In addition to pointing to configuration files using environment 546|variables, you may find it useful (or necessary) to control your 547|configuration values directly from the environment. Flask can be 548|instructed to load all environment variables starting with a specific 549|prefix into the config using :meth:`~flask.Config.from_prefixed_env`. 550| 551|Environment variables can be set in the shell before starting the 552|server: 553| 554|.. tabs:: 555| 556| .. group-tab:: Bash 557| 558| .. code-block:: text 559| 560| $ export FLASK_SECRET_KEY="5f352379324c22463451387a0aec5d2f" 561| $ export FLASK_MAIL_ENABLED=false 562| $ flask run 563| * Running on http://127.0.0.1:5000/ 564| 565| .. group-tab:: Fish 566| 567| .. code-block:: text 568| 569| $ set -x FLASK_SECRET_KEY "5f352379324c22463451387a0aec5d2f" 570| $ set -x FLASK_MAIL_ENABLED false 571| $ flask run 572| * Running on http://127.0.0.1:5000/ 573| 574| .. group-tab:: CMD 575| 576| .. code-block:: text 577| 578| > set FLASK_SECRET_KEY="5f352379324c22463451387a0aec5d2f" 579| > set FLASK_MAIL_ENABLED=false 580| > flask run 581| * Running on http://127.0.0.1:5000/ 582| 583| .. group-tab:: Powershell 584| 585| .. code-block:: text 586| 587| > $env:FLASK_SECRET_KEY = "5f352379324c22463451387a0aec5d2f" 588| > $env:FLASK_MAIL_ENABLED = "false" 589| > flask run 590| * Running on http://127.0.0.1:5000/ 591| 592|The variables can then be loaded and accessed via the config with a key 593|equal to the environment variable name without the prefix i.e. 594| 595|.. code-block:: python 596| 597| app.config.from_prefixed_env() 598| app.config["SECRET_KEY"] # Is "5f352379324c22463451387a0aec5d2f" 599| 600|The prefix is ``FLASK_`` by default. This is configurable via the 601|``prefix`` argument of :meth:`~flask.Config.from_prefixed_env`. 602| 603|Values will be parsed to attempt to convert them to a more specific type 604|than strings. By default :func:`json.loads` is used, so any valid JSON 605|value is possible, including lists and dicts. This is configurable via 606|the ``loads`` argument of :meth:`~flask.Config.from_prefixed_env`. 607| 608|When adding a boolean value with the default JSON parsing, only "true" 609|and "false", lowercase, are valid values. Keep in mind that any 610|non-empty string is considered ``True`` by Python. 611| 612|It is possible to set keys in nested dictionaries by separating the 613|keys with double underscore (``__``). Any intermediate keys that don't 614|exist on the parent dict will be initialized to an empty dict. 615| 616|.. code-block:: text 617| 618| $ export FLASK_MYAPI__credentials__username=user123 619| 620|.. code-block:: python 621| 622| app.config["MYAPI"]["credentials"]["username"] # Is "user123" 623| 624|On Windows, environment variable keys are always uppercase, therefore 625|the above example would end up as ``MYAPI__CREDENTIALS__USERNAME``. 626| 627|For even more config loading features, including merging and 628|case-insensitive Windows support, try a dedicated library such as 629|Dynaconf_, which includes integration with Flask. 630| 631|.. _Dynaconf: https://www.dynaconf.com/ 632| 633| 634|Configuration Best Practices 635|---------------------------- 636| 637|The downside with the approach mentioned earlier is that it makes testing 638|a little harder. There is no single 100% solution for this problem in 639|general, but there are a couple of things you can keep in mind to improve 640|that experience: 641| 642|1. Create your application in a function and register blueprints on it. 643| That way you can create multiple instances of your application with 644| different configurations attached which makes unit testing a lot 645| easier. You can use this to pass in configuration as needed. 646| 647|2. Do not write code that needs the configuration at import time. If you 648| limit yourself to request-only accesses to the configuration you can 649| reconfigure the object later on as needed. 650| 651|3. Make sure to load the configuration very early on, so that 652| extensions can access the configuration when calling ``init_app``. 653| 654| 655|.. _config-dev-prod: 656| 657|Development / Production 658|------------------------ 659| 660|Most applications need more than one configuration. There should be at 661|least separate configurations for the production server and the one used 662|during development. The easiest way to handle this is to use a default 663|configuration that is always loaded and part of the version control, and a 664|separate configuration that overrides the values as necessary as mentioned 665|in the example above:: 666| 667| app = Flask(__name__) 668| app.config.from_object('yourapplication.default_settings') 669| app.config.from_envvar('YOURAPPLICATION_SETTINGS') 670| 671|Then you just have to add a separate :file:`config.py` file and export 672|``YOURAPPLICATION_SETTINGS=/path/to/config.py`` and you are done. However 673|there are alternative ways as well. For example you could use imports or 674|subclassing. 675| 676|What is very popular in the Django world is to make the import explicit in 677|the config file by adding ``from yourapplication.default_settings 678|import *`` to the top of the file and then overriding the changes by hand. 679|You could also inspect an environment variable like 680|``YOURAPPLICATION_MODE`` and set that to `production`, `development` etc 681|and import different hard-coded files based on that. 682| 683|An interesting pattern is also to use classes and inheritance for 684|configuration:: 685| 686| class Config(object): 687| TESTING = False 688| 689| class ProductionConfig(Config): 690| DATABASE_URI = 'mysql://user@localhost/foo' 691| 692| class DevelopmentConfig(Config): 693| DATABASE_URI = "sqlite:////tmp/foo.db" 694| 695| class TestingConfig(Config): 696| DATABASE_URI = 'sqlite:///:memory:' 697| TESTING = True 698| 699|To enable such a config you just have to call into 700|:meth:`~flask.Config.from_object`:: 701| 702| app.config.from_object('configmodule.ProductionConfig') 703| 704|Note that :meth:`~flask.Config.from_object` does not instantiate the class 705|object. If you need to instantiate the class, such as to access a property, 706|then you must do so before calling :meth:`~flask.Config.from_object`:: 707| 708| from configmodule import ProductionConfig 709| app.config.from_object(ProductionConfig()) 710| 711| # Alternatively, import via string: 712| from werkzeug.utils import import_string 713| cfg = import_string('configmodule.ProductionConfig')() 714| app.config.from_object(cfg) 715| 716|Instantiating the configuration object allows you to use ``@property`` in 717|your configuration classes:: 718| 719| class Config(object): 720| """Base config, uses staging database server.""" 721| TESTING = False 722| DB_SERVER = '192.168.1.56' 723| 724| @property 725| def DATABASE_URI(self): # Note: all caps 726| return f"mysql://user@{self.DB_SERVER}/foo" 727| 728| class ProductionConfig(Config): 729| """Uses production database server.""" 730| DB_SERVER = '192.168.19.32' 731| 732| class DevelopmentConfig(Config): 733| DB_SERVER = 'localhost' 734| 735| class TestingConfig(Config): 736| DB_SERVER = 'localhost' 737| DATABASE_URI = 'sqlite:///:memory:' 738| 739|There are many different ways and it's up to you how you want to manage 740|your configuration files. However here a list of good recommendations: 741| 742|- Keep a default configuration in version control. Either populate the 743| config with this default configuration or import it in your own 744| configuration files before overriding values. 745|- Use an environment variable to switch between the configurations. 746| This can be done from outside the Python interpreter and makes 747| development and deployment much easier because you can quickly and 748| easily switch between different configs without having to touch the 749| code at all. If you are working often on different projects you can 750| even create your own script for sourcing that activates a virtualenv 751| and exports the development configuration for you. 752|- Use a tool like `fabric`_ to push code and configuration separately 753| to the production server(s). 754| 755|.. _fabric: https://www.fabfile.org/ 756| 757| 758|.. _instance-folders: 759| 760|Instance Folders 761|---------------- 762| 763|.. versionadded:: 0.8 764| 765|Flask 0.8 introduces instance folders. Flask for a long time made it 766|possible to refer to paths relative to the application's folder directly 767|(via :attr:`Flask.root_path`). This was also how many developers loaded 768|configurations stored next to the application. Unfortunately however this 769|only works well if applications are not packages in which case the root 770|path refers to the contents of the package. 771| 772|With Flask 0.8 a new attribute was introduced: 773|:attr:`Flask.instance_path`. It refers to a new concept called the 774|“instance folder”. The instance folder is designed to not be under 775|version control and be deployment specific. It's the perfect place to 776|drop things that either change at runtime or configuration files. 777| 778|You can either explicitly provide the path of the instance folder when 779|creating the Flask application or you can let Flask autodetect the 780|instance folder. For explicit configuration use the `instance_path` 781|parameter:: 782| 783| app = Flask(__name__, instance_path='/path/to/instance/folder') 784| 785|Please keep in mind that this path *must* be absolute when provided. 786| 787|If the `instance_path` parameter is not provided the following default 788|locations are used: 789| 790|- Uninstalled module:: 791| 792| /myapp.py 793| /instance 794| 795|- Uninstalled package:: 796| 797| /myapp 798| /__init__.py 799| /instance 800| 801|- Installed module or package:: 802| 803| $PREFIX/lib/pythonX.Y/site-packages/myapp 804| $PREFIX/var/myapp-instance 805| 806| ``$PREFIX`` is the prefix of your Python installation. This can be 807| ``/usr`` or the path to your virtualenv. You can print the value of 808| ``sys.prefix`` to see what the prefix is set to. 809| 810|Since the config object provided loading of configuration files from 811|relative filenames we made it possible to change the loading via filenames 812|to be relative to the instance path if wanted. The behavior of relative 813|paths in config files can be flipped between “relative to the application 814|root” (the default) to “relative to instance folder” via the 815|`instance_relative_config` switch to the application constructor:: 816| 817| app = Flask(__name__, instance_relative_config=True) 818| 819|Here is a full example of how to configure Flask to preload the config 820|from a module and then override the config from a file in the instance 821|folder if it exists:: 822| 823| app = Flask(__name__, instance_relative_config=True) 824| app.config.from_object('yourapplication.default_settings') 825| app.config.from_pyfile('application.cfg', silent=True) 826| 827|The path to the instance folder can be found via the 828|:attr:`Flask.instance_path`. Flask also provides a shortcut to open a 829|file from the instance folder with :meth:`Flask.open_instance_resource`. 830| 831|Example usage for both:: 832| 833| filename = os.path.join(app.instance_path, 'application.cfg') 834| with open(filename) as f: 835| config = f.read() 836| 837| # or via open_instance_resource: 838| with app.open_instance_resource('application.cfg') as f: 839| config = f.read() --- END FILE: docs/config.rst --- --- FILE: src/flask/json/tag.py --- 1|""" 2|Tagged JSON 3|~~~~~~~~~~~ 4| 5|A compact representation for lossless serialization of non-standard JSON 6|types. :class:`~flask.sessions.SecureCookieSessionInterface` uses this 7|to serialize the session data, but it may be useful in other places. It's protected by a pin, but that should 11|not be relied on for security. 12| 13|Use an error logging tool, such as Sentry, as described in 14|:ref:`error-logging-tools`, or enable logging and notifications as 15|described in :doc:`/logging`. 16| 17|If you have access to the server, you could add some code to start an 18|external debugger if ``request.remote_addr`` matches your IP. Some IDE 19|debuggers also have a remote mode so breakpoints on the server can be 20|interacted with locally. Only enable a debugger temporarily. 21| 22| 23|The Built-In Debugger 24|--------------------- 25| 26|The built-in Werkzeug development server provides a debugger which shows 27|an interactive traceback in the browser when an unhandled error occurs 28|during a request. This debugger should only be used during development. 29| 30|.. image:: _static/debugger.png 31| :align: center 32| :class: screenshot 33| :alt: screenshot of debugger in action 34| 35|.. warning:: 36| 37| The debugger allows executing arbitrary Python code from the 38| browser. It is protected by a pin, but still represents a major 39| security risk. Do not run the development server or debugger in a 40| production environment. 41| 42|The debugger is enabled by default when the development server is run in debug mode. 43| 44|.. code-block:: text 45| 46| $ flask --app hello run --debug 47| 48|When running from Python code, passing ``debug=True`` enables debug mode, which is 49|mostly equivalent. 50| 51|.. code-block:: python 52| 53| app.run(debug=True) 54| 55|:doc:`/server` and :doc:`/cli` have more information about running the debugger and 56|debug mode. More information about the debugger can be found in the `Werkzeug 57|documentation `__. 58| 59| 60|External Debuggers 61|------------------ 62| 63|External debuggers, such as those provided by IDEs, can offer a more 64|powerful debugging experience than the built-in debugger. They can also 65|be used to step through code during a request before an error is raised, 66|or if no error is raised. Some even have a remote mode so you can debug 67|code running on another machine. 68| 69|When using an external debugger, the app should still be in debug mode, otherwise Flask 70|turns unhandled errors into generic 500 error pages. However, the built-in debugger and 71|reloader should be disabled so they don't interfere with the external debugger. 72| 73|.. code-block:: text 74| 75| $ flask --app hello run --debug --no-debugger --no-reload 76| 77|When running from Python: 78| 79|.. code-block:: python 80| 81| app.run(debug=True, use_debugger=False, use_reloader=False) 82| 83|Disabling these isn't required, an external debugger will continue to work with the 84|following caveats. 85| 86|- If the built-in debugger is not disabled, it will catch unhandled exceptions before 87| the external debugger can. 88|- If the reloader is not disabled, it could cause an unexpected reload if code changes 89| during a breakpoint. 90|- The development server will still catch unhandled exceptions if the built-in 91| debugger is disabled, otherwise it would crash on any error. When serving 5|your application with one of the WSGI servers listed in :doc:`index`, it 6|is often good or necessary to put a dedicated HTTP server in front of 7|it. This "reverse proxy" can handle incoming requests, TLS, and other 8|security and performance concerns better than the WSGI server. 9| 10|httpd can be installed using your system package manager, or a pre-built 11|executable for Windows. Installing and running httpd itself is outside 12|the scope of this doc. This page outlines the basics of configuring 13|httpd to proxy your application. Be sure to read its documentation to 14|understand what features are available. 15| 16|.. _Apache httpd: https://httpd.apache.org/ 17| 18| 19|Domain Name 20|----------- 21| 22|Acquiring and configuring a domain name is outside the scope of this 23|doc. In general, you will buy a domain name from a registrar, pay for 24|server space with a hosting provider, and then point your registrar 25|at the hosting provider's name servers. 26| 27|To simulate this, you can also edit your ``hosts`` file, located at 28|``/etc/hosts`` on Linux. Add a line that associates a name with the 29|local IP. 30| 31|Modern Linux systems may be configured to treat any domain name that 32|ends with ``.localhost`` like this without adding it to the ``hosts`` 33|file. 34| 35|.. code-block:: python 36| :caption: ``/etc/hosts`` 37| 38| 127.0.0.1 hello.localhost 39| 40| 41|Configuration 42|------------- 43| 44|The httpd configuration is located at ``/etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf`` on 45|Linux. It may be different depending on your operating system. Check the 46|docs and look for ``httpd.conf``. 47| 48|Remove or comment out any existing ``DocumentRoot`` directive. Add the 49|config lines below. We'll assume the WSGI server is listening locally at 50|``http://127.0.0.1:8000``. 51| 52|.. code-block:: apache 53| :caption: ``/etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf`` 54| 55| LoadModule proxy_module modules/mod_proxy.so 56| LoadModule proxy_http_module modules/mod_proxy_http.so 57| ProxyPass / http://127.0.0.1:8000/ 58| RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Proto http 59| RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Prefix / 60| 61|The ``LoadModule`` lines might already exist. If so, make sure they are 62|uncommented instead of adding them manually. 63| 64|Then :doc:`proxy_fix` so that your application uses the ``X-Forwarded`` 65|headers. ``X-Forwarded-For`` and ``X-Forwarded-Host`` are automatically 66|set by ``ProxyPass``. --- END FILE: docs/deploying/apache-httpd.rst --- --- FILE: src/flask/sansio/app.py --- 1|from __future__ import annotations 2| 3|import collections.abc as cabc 4|import logging 5|import os 6|import sys 7|import typing as t 8|from datetime import timedelta 9|from itertools import chain 10| 11|from werkzeug.exceptions import Aborter 12|from werkzeug.exceptions import BadRequest 13|from werkzeug.exceptions import BadRequestKeyError 14|from werkzeug.routing import BuildError 15|from werkzeug.routing import Map 16|from werkzeug.routing import Rule 17|from werkzeug.sansio.response import Response 18|from werkzeug.utils import cached_property 19|from werkzeug.utils import redirect as _wz_redirect 20| 21|from .. import typing as ft 22|from ..config import Config 23|from ..config import ConfigAttribute 24|from ..ctx import _AppCtxGlobals 25|from ..helpers import _split_blueprint_path 26|from ..helpers import get_debug_flag 27|from ..json.provider import DefaultJSONProvider 28|from ..json.provider import JSONProvider 29|from ..logging import create_logger 30|from ..templating import DispatchingJinjaLoader 31|from ..templating import Environment 32|from .scaffold import _endpoint_from_view_func 33|from .scaffold import find_package 34|from .scaffold import Scaffold 35|from .scaffold import setupmethod 36| 37|if t.TYPE_CHECKING: # Be sure to read its 14|`documentation`_ and use ``gunicorn --help`` to understand what features 15|are available. 16| 17|.. _Gunicorn: https://gunicorn.org/ 18|.. _documentation: https://docs.gunicorn.org/ 19| 20| 21|Installing 22|---------- 23| 24|Gunicorn is easy to install, as it does not require external 25|dependencies or compilation. It runs on Windows only under WSL. 26| 27|Create a virtualenv, install your application, then install 28|``gunicorn``. 29| 30|.. code-block:: text 31| 32| $ cd hello-app 33| $ python -m venv .venv 34| $ . .venv/bin/activate 35| $ pip install . # install your application 36| $ pip install gunicorn 37| 38| 39|Running 40|------- 41| 42|The only required argument to Gunicorn tells it how to load your Flask 43|application. The syntax is ``{module_import}:{app_variable}``. 44|``module_import`` is the dotted import name to the module with your 45|application. ``app_variable`` is the variable with the application. It 46|can also be a function call (with any arguments) if you're using the 47|app factory pattern. 48| 49|.. code-block:: text 50| 51| # equivalent to 'from hello import app' 52| $ gunicorn -w 4 'hello:app' 53| 54| # equivalent to 'from hello import create_app; create_app()' 55| $ gunicorn -w 4 'hello:create_app()' 56| 57| Starting gunicorn 20.1.0 58| Listening at: http://127.0.0.1:8000 (x) 59| Using worker: sync 60| Booting worker with pid: x 61| Booting worker with pid: x 62| Booting worker with pid: x 63| Booting worker with pid: x 64| 65|The ``-w`` option specifies the number of processes to run; a starting 66|value could be ``CPU * 2``. The default is only 1 worker, which is 67|probably not what you want for the default worker type. 68| 69|Logs for each request aren't shown by default, only worker info and 70|errors are shown. To show access logs on stdout, use the 71|``--access-logfile=-`` option. 72| 73| 74|Binding Externally 75|------------------ 76| 77|Gunicorn should not be run as root because it would cause your 78|application code to run as root, which is not secure. However, this 79|means it will not be possible to bind to port 80 or 443. Instead, a 80|reverse proxy such as :doc:`nginx` or :doc:`apache-httpd` should be used 81|in front of Gunicorn. 82| 83|You can bind to all external IPs on a non-privileged port using the 84|``-b 0.0.0.0`` option. Don't do this when using a reverse proxy setup, 85|otherwise it will be possible to bypass the proxy. 86| 87|.. code-block:: text 88| 89| $ gunicorn -w 4 -b 0.0.0.0 'hello:create_app()' 90| Listening at: http://0.0.0.0:8000 (x) 91| 92|``0.0.0.0`` is not a valid address to navigate to, you'd use a specific 93|IP address in your browser. 94| 95| 96|Async with gevent 97|----------------- 98| 99|The default sync worker is appropriate for most use cases. If you need numerous, 100|long running, concurrent connections, Gunicorn provides an asynchronous worker 101|using `gevent`_. This is not the same as Python's ``async/await``, or the ASGI 102|server spec. See :doc:`/gevent` for more information about enabling it in your 103|application. 104| 105|.. _gevent: https://www.gevent.org/ 106| 107|When using gevent, greenlet>=1.0 is required. When using PyPy, PyPy>=7.3.7 is 108|required. 109| 110|.. code-block:: text 111| 112| $ gunicorn -k gevent 'hello:create_app()' 113| Starting gunicorn 20.1.0 114| Listening at: http://127.0.0.1:8000 (x) 115| Using worker: gevent 116| Booting worker with pid: x --- END FILE: docs/deploying/gunicorn.rst --- --- FILE: docs/license.rst --- 1|BSD-3-Clause License 2|==================== 3| 4|.. literalinclude:: ../LICENSE.txt 5| :language: text --- END FILE: docs/license.rst --- --- FILE: docs/patterns/jquery.rst --- 1|:orphan: 2| 3|AJAX with jQuery 4|================ 5| 6|Obsolete, see :doc:`/patterns/javascript` instead. --- END FILE: docs/patterns/jquery.rst --- FILES_END
